cim: From Market Women to Female Professionals: Can Artificial Intelligence Transform Women's Economic Lives in Ghana?
cim_eredeti: From Market Women to Female Professionals: Can Artificial Intelligence Transform Women's Economic Lives in Ghana?
szoveg_eredeti:
Artificial intelligence is gradually changing how people conduct business, perform their professional duties and earn a living. What once appeared to be a technological development reserved for advanced economies is increasingly becoming part of everyday life in Ghana. From banking and education to healthcare, agriculture and trading, digital technologies are opening new possibilities for economic growth. Yet, an important question deserves attention. Can artificial intelligence genuinely improve the economic lives of Ghanaian women, particularly those whose livelihoods depend on small businesses, informal trading and professional employment?

This question is especially relevant because women occupy an important place in Ghana's economy. Walk through Makola Market in Accra, Kejetia in Kumasi or any major trading centre across the country, and one cannot overlook the determination of women who sustain businesses, support families and contribute to local economic activity. Beyond the markets, women serve as teachers, nurses, bankers, administrators, entrepreneurs and professionals in many other fields. Their daily contributions demonstrate that women's economic advancement is inseparable from Ghana's broader development.

However, many of these women continue to work under difficult conditions. Limited access to affordable credit, inadequate business information, rising operating costs, unequal employment opportunities and competing family responsibilities often restrict their economic progress. Artificial intelligence may not resolve all these challenges, but its responsible application could provide practical opportunities for improving productivity, expanding businesses and strengthening women's financial independence.

For many Ghanaian market women, business decisions are shaped by personal experience, customer relationships and knowledge acquired over several years. These traditional strengths remain valuable. However, artificial intelligence could complement them by making useful business information more accessible.

Consider a woman selling tomatoes, onions or smoked fish in a busy market. Her business depends on knowing what customers need, how much stock to purchase and when prices are likely to change. With access to appropriate digital tools, she could receive assistance in monitoring sales, organising business records, comparing prices and identifying purchasing patterns. Such information could help reduce avoidable losses and improve financial planning.

A dressmaker, hairdresser or food vendor could similarly benefit from digital applications that assist with customer communication, advertising, appointment scheduling and basic bookkeeping. Women operating small enterprises could use these tools to promote their products beyond their immediate communities and establish relationships with customers in other parts of Ghana.

Nevertheless, technology must respond to the realities of the people expected to use it. Many market women have limited time for formal training, while others may not be comfortable with complicated applications or written instructions in English. Affordable tools that support familiar Ghanaian languages, simple instructions and practical business activities would make artificial intelligence more useful to these entrepreneurs.

The market woman does not necessarily need to understand how an artificial intelligence system is developed. What matters is whether she can use it confidently to improve her business and increase her earnings.

Artificial intelligence also offers considerable opportunities for women working in Ghana's formal employment sector. Female teachers can use appropriate digital tools to prepare instructional materials, develop learning activities and support students with different educational needs. Healthcare professionals may benefit from systems that assist with medical documentation, information management and clinical decision support, subject to professional oversight.

Women working in banking, administration, accounting and other service industries can use artificial intelligence to organise information, improve communication and manage routine assignments more efficiently. Entrepreneurs and professionals can also explore new income opportunities through digital consulting, online education, content development and technology related services.

These developments are important because professional advancement increasingly depends on the ability to acquire and apply new skills. A woman who understands how to use emerging technologies responsibly may be better positioned to adapt to changes in her workplace and pursue new career opportunities.

However, the benefits will not be automatic. Artificial intelligence is also changing the nature of employment, particularly in occupations involving repetitive administrative and information processing tasks. Some responsibilities may be automated, while others will require additional technological skills. Women who are unable to access relevant training could consequently face difficulties maintaining their competitiveness in the labour market.

This makes continuous professional development essential. Employers, universities and professional associations should provide accessible training that enables women to understand artificial intelligence, recognise its limitations and apply it effectively within their professions.

Although the opportunities are encouraging, Ghana must confront a difficult reality. Not every woman has the same opportunity to participate in the digital economy.

For a woman in an urban community with reliable internet access, a suitable digital device and the financial means to acquire new skills, artificial intelligence may offer exciting possibilities. For another woman in a rural community struggling with connectivity, unreliable electricity or limited household income, these opportunities may remain distant.

The cost of internet services, smartphones, computers and training programmes can discourage participation. Educational inequalities and limited exposure to technology may create additional difficulties, particularly for women who have spent much of their working lives in the informal economy.

These differences matter because technological progress can widen existing economic inequalities when access is concentrated among those who are already relatively advantaged. If Ghana celebrates artificial intelligence without addressing these barriers, the women who could benefit most from improved economic opportunities may become the least able to access them.

Artificial intelligence must therefore be introduced as a practical development opportunity rather than an expensive privilege reserved for highly educated professionals and financially established businesses.

As women become more involved in digital activities, attention must also be given to their safety and economic security. Fraudulent investment schemes, misleading online advertisements, privacy violations and digitally manipulated information can expose women to financial losses and reputational harm.

Small business operators may be particularly vulnerable when they rely on unfamiliar digital platforms without adequate information about their risks. Likewise, professionals must understand that artificial intelligence can generate inaccurate information and should not be trusted without appropriate verification.
